job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed the text as provided (as amended by the Oct. 6 manager's amendment). I haven't compared it against the introduced version. The constitutional items are issue-spotting, so have counsel or CRS confirm them before we publish anything.

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), fixed compute threshold.** A hard-coded 10^26 operations has no mechanism for adjustment. Algorithmic and hardware efficiency gains mean a system with dangerous capabilities could be built under the line, and the Secretary has no authority to lower it.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "single training run."** The term is undefined, so a developer could split work across multiple runs, restart from checkpoints, or chain pretraining, fine-tuning, and continued training, each staying under the threshold. The text doesn't say whether compute from earlier runs on the same model counts.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), how compute is counted.** It doesn't say what counts toward the total: reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, compute inherited from a base model, or inference-time compute. It also doesn't say who measures or verifies the figure, which makes the threshold hard to prove in an enforcement action.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A)–(B), "artificial intelligence model" and "system."** Neither is defined. It's unclear how the bill treats ensembles, distilled models, agentic systems built from several models, or a below-threshold model trained on outputs of a covered one.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The Act never says which Secretary. Sec. 6 refers to the Secretary of State and Sec. 4 to the Department of Commerce, so a challenger could argue the determination power is undefined or that any determination is invalid.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), the capability standard.** "Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks" has no benchmark, baseline human, or definition of "most" or "cognitive tasks." Reasonable people, and courts, could read it very differently.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), no determination process.** There is no deadline, notice, rulemaking, public list, evidence standard, or review mechanism. A developer can't know in advance whether its system is covered, and it's unclear whether a determination applies retroactively to work already done.

8. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** It covers only citizens and State-organized corporations. It omits lawful permanent residents, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and unincorporated associations. It also omits foreign subsidiaries of U.S. firms, and it's unclear whether D.C. and territorial entities count as "State" organizations.

9. **Sec. 2(3), "advanced AI chip" and "data center."** Both are undefined, with no performance specification or update mechanism. Because the registry depends on the term, the facility count is open to dispute.

10. **Sec. 2(3), chip-count threshold.** A raw count of more than 50,000 chips ignores chip performance. Operators could stay under it by using several sites of 50,000 or fewer, using distributed training across sites, or buying fewer, more powerful chips.

11. **Sec. 2 generally, "person" and government actors.** "Person" is never defined, and the Act doesn't say whether it reaches federal agencies, the military, intelligence agencies, or their contractors. It has no national-security exemption, and silence invites disputes either way.

## Prohibition (Sec. 3)

12. **Sec. 3(a), "train, develop, or deploy."** None of the verbs is defined. "Develop" could sweep in basic research, and "deploy" doesn't say whether it covers API access, hosting, open-weight release, internal use, or importing a foreign-trained model.

13. **Sec. 3(a), when a system becomes "covered."** Under Sec. 2(1)(A), a model is covered only after it is trained above the threshold, but Sec. 3(a) bans "training" a covered system. It's unclear whether a run is unlawful while underway, only when it crosses the line, or when it is planned, and there is no attempt or planning provision.

14. **Sec. 3(a), reach.** The bill covers "any person in the United States" and U.S. persons anywhere. A foreign company with no U.S. presence that serves U.S. users from abroad may fall outside it, and foreign subsidiaries of U.S. firms escape through the narrow Sec. 2(2) definition.

15. **Sec. 3(a), ancillary actors.** It doesn't address cloud and compute providers, financiers, chip suppliers, or redistributors of released model weights. There is no knowing-facilitation or aiding-and-abetting provision for civil liability, so enforcement would depend on reaching the direct trainer.

16. **Sec. 3(b), "training began."** The term is undefined, and no documentation or registration is required for pre-enactment systems. Developers have an incentive to start large runs before enactment, or to backdate them, and the Act doesn't say who bears the burden of proving the start date.

17. **Sec. 3(b), scope of the grandfather clause.** It exempts the system from all of Sec. 3(a), including deployment, with no cap on further compute. Existing systems could be scaled, continually retrained, fine-tuned, or released as "versions" of the same system, and a long-running training effort could continue indefinitely.

18. **Sec. 3(b) / Sec. 5(a) / Sec. 8, timing gap.** Grandfathering turns on enactment, but the Act takes effect 180 days later. A run begun in that window is not grandfathered, yet the prohibition isn't yet in force, and the text doesn't say whether it must stop on the effective date.

19. **Sec. 3(c), safety-evaluation exemption.** "Activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation" is undefined and judged by purpose. A developer could claim that training or running a covered system is for evaluation, and the exemption sets no limits on compute, duration, or deployment.

20. **Sec. 3(c), no oversight of the exemption.** It requires no notice to the government, approval, independent evaluator, security standard, or record-keeping. It's self-declared and unverifiable, and it could swallow the prohibition.

## Registry (Sec. 4)

21. **Sec. 4(a), "operator."** The Act doesn't say whether this means the facility owner, the lessee, or a cloud tenant running workloads. That matters because the operator must certify workloads it may not control or be able to see.

22. **Sec. 4(a), no deadline or implementing authority.** There is no registration deadline, no required content, and no grant of rulemaking power to Commerce. The registry can't function without implementing rules, and nothing requires Commerce to write them.

23. **Sec. 4(b), report content.** "Describing the computing workloads" sets no standard. Reports needn't identify models, customers, compute used, or training-run start dates, so they may be useless for detecting a Sec. 3 violation or testing a grandfathering claim.

24. **Sec. 4(b), self-certification without verification.** The Act gives Commerce no audit, inspection, subpoena, or data-access authority. Reports arrive quarterly, so a violation could go undetected for months.

25. **Sec. 4, no penalty for registry violations.** The only penalties (Sec. 5) attach to violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false certification carries no stated consequence beyond whatever general false-statement law might apply.

26. **Sec. 4, coverage gaps.** Facilities with 50,000 or fewer chips, and foreign facilities, escape reporting. Commerce's authority over facilities abroad is unclear even for U.S.-owned ones.

27. **Sec. 4, confidentiality.** The Act has no provisions protecting trade secrets or sensitive workload data, restricting FOIA release, or securing the submissions. Operators could resist reporting on those grounds.

## Penalties (Sec. 5)

28. **Sec. 5, no enforcing authority or procedure.** The Act doesn't say who investigates, assesses, or sues for penalties: the Attorney General, Commerce, or both. It provides no notice, hearing, or appeal process, and no private right of action.

29. **Sec. 5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs."** It's unclear whether a multi-month training run, or ongoing deployment, is one continuing violation or one per day. A $1 million cap with no minimum, factors, or scaling by size may be a tolerable cost for the largest firms, given what frontier training costs.

30. **Sec. 5(a), "on or after the date of enactment."** This conflicts with Sec. 8's 180-day delay, since Sec. 3 isn't in effect until then. It reads as penalties for conduct that isn't yet unlawful, and that ambiguity gives defendants a challenge on fair notice and retroactivity.

31. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** The mental state is undefined. Combined with the vague capability prong in Sec. 2(1)(B), prosecutors would have to prove a defendant knew its system was covered, and defendants would argue they couldn't have known.

32. **Sec. 5(b), criminal fines and remedies.** Fines "under title 18" default to the general caps in 18 U.S.C. § 3571 (as I recall, $250,000 for individuals and $500,000 for organizations, or twice the gain or loss), which could be lower than the civil exposure. The Act also provides no injunctions, cease-and-desist orders, forfeiture of chips or model weights, or officer liability.

33. **Sec. 5(a), adjudication forum.** If civil penalties were imposed administratively, defendants could raise a Seventh Amendment challenge under *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024). The Act doesn't say whether penalties are assessed in federal court.

## International agreement, duration, effective date (Secs. 6–8)

34. **Sec. 6, "seek to negotiate."** The duty is to try, not to conclude, and the 18-month deadline attaches to negotiation. There's no reporting requirement, consequence for failure, or definition of "equivalent" prohibitions.

35. **Sec. 6, no treaty or implementation path.** The text doesn't say whether an agreement would be a treaty (Senate advice and consent) or an executive agreement. It doesn't address what happens to the domestic ban if other states decline, which is the offshoring problem.

36. **Sec. 7(a), the NASEM report.** The Act doesn't require NASEM to produce a report, set a timeline or funding, or define "safely." The path out of the prohibition depends on a nongovernmental body that Congress hasn't directed to act.

37. **Sec. 7(a), joint resolution mechanics.** A joint resolution must be presented to the President, so a veto requires a two-thirds override. There are no expedited Senate procedures, so the Senate filibuster applies. The mechanism is all-or-nothing, with no partial lifting for categories or uses.

38. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), conflicting duration.** Sec. 7(a) is open-ended while Sec. 7(b) ends the Act after 10 years, and the text doesn't say which controls. There is no savings clause for pending enforcement or prosecutions, so sunset could wipe out cases for conduct during the Act's life. And since Sec. 8 delays effect 180 days, the ban is in force only about 9.5 years.

39. **Sec. 8, no phase-in.** Everything takes effect at once, with no staging for the registry, no deadline for Commerce to stand up systems, and no interim reporting. The 180-day window is also a period when firms can start or accelerate runs.

## Cross-cutting issues that make the bill easier to challenge

40. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes the Secretary-determination prong (Sec. 2(1)(B)) or the "develop" language, nothing says the rest of the Act survives.

41. **Vagueness and nondelegation (Secs. 2(1)(B), 3, 5(b)).** Criminal liability keyed to an undefined, agency-determined capability standard invites a fair-notice challenge. The Act gives the Secretary no "intelligible principle" to guide the determination, which supports a nondelegation argument.

42. **First Amendment (Sec. 3(a)).** Banning "develop" could reach research, publication, and code or model weights, which some courts have treated as protected expression. A narrower definition of prohibited conduct would help.

43. **Commerce Clause (Sec. 3(a)).** The prohibition has no jurisdictional element and no findings tying the covered activity to interstate or foreign commerce. A purely intrastate training run could be a test case.

44. **No findings or purpose section.** "Superintelligence" appears in the title but not in the operative text, and the Act includes no statement of purpose or congressional findings. That weakens the legislative record courts use to interpret and uphold the Act.

45. **No judicial review or implementation provisions.** The Act doesn't address review of Secretary determinations, rulemaking authority, appropriations for Commerce or the enforcing agency, or whistleblower protection.

46. **Relationship to other law.** The Act doesn't address preemption of state AI laws or its interaction with existing export controls.

## Likely most significant for coverage

For your markup preview, I'd flag these as most consequential:

- **Enforcement structure:** items 25 and 28, since no one is designated to enforce and the registry has no penalty.
- **Grandfather and exemption scope:** items 16, 17, and 19.
- **Threshold evasion:** items 1, 2, and 10.
- **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8 conflict:** item 30.
- **Undefined "Secretary" and the Sec. 2(1)(B) standard:** items 5 through 7.

If it would help, I can turn this into a one-page explainer or a table of issues with proposed amendments that members might raise at the markup. Keeping with CPR's approach, I'd frame those as questions committee members might ask rather than recommendations.
